title: Designing a patient portal people actually use
summary: Most portals are built around the structure of the record rather than the questions people arrive with. Reversing that order changes almost every screen.
body:
Ask someone why they opened their patient portal and the answer is rarely to browse a record. It is to find out when an appointment is, whether a result has come back, or what a clinician meant by something said in a hurry.

Portals organised around clinical data structures make those questions hard to answer. The record is arranged by document type and encounter, so a person looking for one number navigates three levels of an information architecture designed for a different reader.

Reordering the interface around intent means the landing view answers the three most common questions first, and the full record stays one step away for the smaller number of people who want it. The underlying data does not change; only the order in which it is offered does.

seo.title: Designing a patient portal people actually use
seo.description: Most portals are built around the structure of the record rather than the questions people arrive with. Reversing that order changes almost every screen.

title: Plain language in clinical communication
summary: A practical guide to writing appointment reminders, result notifications and care instructions that do not require a clinical vocabulary to understand.
body:
Written communication from a health service is often produced by clinicians for clinicians and then sent to patients unchanged. The result is accurate and unreadable.

Plain language is not simplification of the underlying medicine. It is choosing the shortest accurate word, putting the action first, and stating what happens next. An instruction that begins with what the reader must do is followed more reliably than one that begins with the reasoning behind it.

This guide covers sentence length, the ordering of actions and caveats, how to express uncertainty honestly, and why reading-age tools are a starting point rather than a target.

seo.title: Plain language in clinical communication
seo.description: A practical guide to writing appointment reminders, result notifications and care instructions that do not require a clinical vocabulary to understand.

title: Reducing the cost of digital intake
summary: Pre-visit forms are the most abandoned surface in digital health. Adaptive questioning and re-use of known answers address most of the drop-off.
body:
Digital intake asks people to supply information a service often already holds. Every question that could have been pre-filled is a reason to abandon the form, and abandonment moves the work back to the clinic reception desk.

Two changes account for most of the improvement. The first is adaptive questioning: branching on earlier answers so nobody is asked about conditions irrelevant to their visit. The second is persistence, so a returning patient confirms rather than retypes.

The remaining friction is usually structural. Forms that must be completed in one sitting fail people who are interrupted, and a save-and-resume path costs little to build.

seo.title: Reducing the cost of digital intake
seo.description: Pre-visit forms are the most abandoned surface in digital health. Adaptive questioning and re-use of known answers address most of the drop-off.

title: What connected care actually requires
summary: Connected care is often described as a technology problem. Most of the difficulty is in agreeing what a shared record should contain and who maintains it.
body:
The phrase connected care suggests that the obstacle is a missing integration. In practice the harder question is editorial: which parts of a record are shared, at what level of detail, and who is accountable when two sources disagree.

Technical exchange standards answer the transport question and leave the governance question open. A shared medication list is only useful if there is agreement about which system is authoritative when entries conflict.

Programmes that begin with governance and then choose transport tend to arrive faster than those that begin by connecting systems and discover the disagreements afterwards.

seo.title: What connected care actually requires
seo.description: Connected care is often described as a technology problem. Most of the difficulty is in agreeing what a shared record should contain and who maintains it.

title: Remote consultations beyond video
summary: Video is the visible part of remote care. The scheduling, triage and follow-up around it determine whether it saves anyone time.
body:
A remote consultation that requires the same preparation, the same waiting and the same follow-up phone calls as an in-person visit has moved the location of the appointment without changing its cost.

The gains come from the surrounding workflow: triage that routes a question to the right response, asynchronous messaging for issues that do not need a synchronous conversation, and structured follow-up that does not depend on a callback.

Video then becomes one option among several rather than the default, chosen when seeing someone genuinely changes the clinical decision.

seo.title: Remote consultations beyond video
seo.description: Video is the visible part of remote care. The scheduling, triage and follow-up around it determine whether it saves anyone time.

title: Measuring digital health without vanity metrics
summary: Registration counts and app downloads say little about whether care improved. A short set of measures tied to clinical and operational outcomes says more.
body:
Digital health programmes are frequently reported through adoption figures. Registrations, downloads and monthly active users are easy to collect and almost impossible to interpret, because none of them describe whether anything got better.

More useful measures tend to be smaller in number and harder to collect: time from request to appointment, proportion of appointments attended, proportion of intake completed before arrival, and the volume of administrative contact a patient must initiate.

This piece sets out a minimal measurement set and, more importantly, which measures to stop reporting.

seo.title: Measuring digital health without vanity metrics
seo.description: Registration counts and app downloads say little about whether care improved. A short set of measures tied to clinical and operational outcomes says more.

title: A practical introduction to FHIR R4
summary: What FHIR resources are, how they relate, and where implementations usually diverge in ways that break interoperability in practice.
body:
FHIR describes healthcare data as resources with defined relationships, exchanged over ordinary web protocols. That much is straightforward, and it is where most introductions stop.

The difficulty appears in the extension points. Two systems can both claim conformance while representing the same concept differently, because the specification permits local extension and the profiles that constrain it are chosen per implementation.

This introduction walks through the resources most commonly exchanged, then spends most of its length on profiling, terminology binding, and the questions worth asking before agreeing an integration is complete.

seo.title: A practical introduction to FHIR R4
seo.description: What FHIR resources are, how they relate, and where implementations usually diverge in ways that break interoperability in practice.

title: When an integration is not interoperability
summary: A working point-to-point interface and an interoperable system are different things. The distinction becomes expensive at the third connection.
body:
A single interface between two systems can be built quickly by agreeing a format between two teams. It works, and it is not interoperability, because the agreement lives in the connection rather than in a standard.

The cost appears when a third system arrives. Each new participant needs its own agreement, and the number of interfaces grows faster than the number of systems.

Standards-based exchange trades a slower first connection for a flat cost per additional one. The decision is not technical preference; it is a judgement about how many connections the programme will eventually need.

seo.title: When an integration is not interoperability
seo.description: A working point-to-point interface and an interoperable system are different things. The distinction becomes expensive at the third connection.

title: Scheduling that respects clinical capacity
summary: Open booking against a clinical calendar fails quietly unless the model understands appointment types, preparation time and the limits of a working day.
body:
Exposing a clinical calendar for direct booking is technically simple and clinically risky. A calendar slot is not a unit of interchangeable time: appointment types differ in length, in preparation and in what must follow them.

A scheduling model that ignores those differences produces days that look full and are unworkable, which erodes clinical trust in the system faster than any other failure.

The workable version encodes appointment types, buffers and daily limits, and treats clinician-defined constraints as authoritative rather than advisory.

seo.title: Scheduling that respects clinical capacity
seo.description: Open booking against a clinical calendar fails quietly unless the model understands appointment types, preparation time and the limits of a working day.

title: Reducing missed appointments
summary: Missed appointments are usually treated as a reminder problem. Access, timing and transport explain more of the variance than notification volume.
body:
The standard response to missed appointments is to send more reminders. Reminder volume has a measurable effect and reaches its limit quickly, after which additional messages mostly annoy the people who were going to attend anyway.

Larger factors tend to sit upstream: how far ahead the appointment was booked, whether the time is reachable given work and transport, and how easy it is to reschedule rather than simply not attend.

Making rescheduling a one-step action often does more than any change to notification, because it converts a non-attendance into a future appointment.

seo.title: Reducing missed appointments
seo.description: Missed appointments are usually treated as a reminder problem. Access, timing and transport explain more of the variance than notification volume.

title: Designing role-based access for clinical teams
summary: Least-privilege access is straightforward to state and difficult to model, because clinical roles overlap and cover for one another.
body:
Role-based access assumes roles are stable and separable. Clinical teams are neither: staff cover for colleagues, rotate between services, and need occasional access outside their usual scope for legitimate reasons.

Systems that model roles too rigidly are worked around, usually by sharing credentials, which removes the audit trail the model existed to protect.

A workable design combines a conservative default with an explicit, logged break-glass path, so unusual access is possible, visible and reviewable rather than impossible and therefore circumvented.

seo.title: Designing role-based access for clinical teams
seo.description: Least-privilege access is straightforward to state and difficult to model, because clinical roles overlap and cover for one another.

title: What audit logging should capture
summary: An audit log that records everything is as unusable as one that records nothing. Capturing intent alongside action is what makes review possible.
body:
Audit logs in clinical systems frequently record that a record was opened, by whom and when. That is enough to prove access occurred and not enough to judge whether it should have.

Reviewable logs capture the context of access: the care relationship in effect, the workflow the user was in, and whether the access followed a break-glass path.

This piece covers what to capture, what to exclude for privacy reasons, retention considerations, and why logs intended for review need to be readable by people who are not engineers.

seo.title: What audit logging should capture
seo.description: An audit log that records everything is as unusable as one that records nothing. Capturing intent alongside action is what makes review possible.

title: Assisted clinical documentation and the review step
summary: Automatically drafted notes save time only if the review step is designed as carefully as the generation step.
body:
Drafting a clinical note automatically moves the work from composition to verification. That is a real saving when verification is quicker than writing, and a real risk when the draft is plausible enough to be approved without close reading.

Design decisions determine which of those happens: whether the draft highlights what it inferred rather than heard, whether uncertain content is marked, and whether approval requires an action proportionate to the responsibility being taken.

The clinician remains accountable for the note. The interface should make that accountability easy to exercise rather than easy to skip.

seo.title: Assisted clinical documentation and the review step
seo.description: Automatically drafted notes save time only if the review step is designed as carefully as the generation step.

title: Accessibility is a clinical requirement
summary: In health services the people least able to use an inaccessible interface are frequently the people who need it most.
body:
Accessibility in most sectors is a question of reach. In health it is closer to a clinical one, because impairment and long-term condition are correlated, and the population using a health service is not the population that tested it.

The practical implications are ordinary: semantic structure, keyboard operability, sufficient contrast, content that survives magnification, and forms that state their errors clearly. None of it is exotic, and all of it is routinely missing.

This piece sets out the checks worth running on every release, which of them can be automated, and the roughly two thirds of issues that automated tooling will not find.

seo.title: Accessibility is a clinical requirement
seo.description: In health services the people least able to use an inaccessible interface are frequently the people who need it most.
